items.stem: The data layer in GTM is best described as:

options.text: A visual report of tag performance
options.rationale: That is not what the data layer is; it is a data structure, not a report.

options.text: A structured object holding information for tags, triggers and variables to use
options.rationale: Correct: the data layer is a structured store of values GTM reads from.
The snippet loads GTM; the data layer is the structured data it reads.
The data layer is part of the page/GTM, not a GA property.

items.explanation: Correct: the data layer is a structured store of values GTM reads from.

items.stem: Before publishing a new tag to production, the recommended step is to:

options.text: Publish immediately and watch live reports
options.rationale: Publishing untested tags risks broken or duplicated tracking in production.

options.text: Use Preview and debug mode to confirm the tag fires correctly
options.rationale: Correct: Preview mode verifies firing and data before going live.
Deleting the container is unnecessary and harmful.
Disabling the data layer would break tracking, not test it.

items.explanation: Correct: Preview mode verifies firing and data before going live.

items.stem: Which TWO are good GTM governance and consent practices? (Select TWO)

options.text: Hold non-essential marketing tags until the user grants consent
options.rationale: Correct: consent-aware firing is required for privacy compliance.

options.text: Use clear naming conventions and document tags for maintainability
options.rationale: Correct: naming and documentation keep a container auditable.

options.text: Give every team member full publish access by default
options.rationale: Unrestricted publish access undermines governance and control.

options.text: Fire all tags on page load regardless of consent
options.rationale: Ignoring consent is a privacy and compliance failure.

items.explanation: Correct: consent-aware firing is required for privacy compliance.; Correct: naming and documentation keep a container auditable.
